analysis.title: Global Metals Weekly: The battle for critical minerals
key_insights: China's copper demand contracted 8% YoY in September, driven by a pullback in grid spending (FAI in electricity and heat generation fell 7% YoY in August), but declines have started bottoming out.
China's physical copper market is tight despite weak demand: domestic inventories have declined gradually this year and Shanghai premia hit an all-time high as consumers struggle to source units.
Profitable US warehouse-financing deals pulled spare copper into North America, leaving World ex-US undersupplied. Tight mine supply contributed, but financing profitability is the bigger factor.

LME copper forward curves moved into deeper backwardation. A single trader holds 50-79% of cash positions, so the market can be squeezed with little capital. BofA keeps seeing copper upside into next year despite soft Chinese consumption.

Hyperscale data centres are considerably more metals intensive than enterprise sites: relative intensity is 1x for enterprise, 1.3-1.5x for colocation, 1.8-2.2x for cloud hyperscalers and 2.5-3.0x for AI hyperscalers.
Hyperscale copper intensity is 23,900 t/GW vs 10,600 t/GW for enterprise. Silver intensity is 708,000 oz/GW for hyperscale vs 318,000 oz/GW for enterprise. Aluminium is 6,200 t/GW vs 2,600 t/GW.
BofA projects data centre capacity rising from 114 GW in 2025 to 241 GW in 2030, and data centre electricity from 485 TWh to 1,025 TWh (1.72% to 3.05% of total consumption).
Grid, data centres/AI and EVs hold roughly 40% of copper demand and are expected to deliver as much demand growth in 2026-30 as the whole market did over the past decade.

Caveats to the data centre metals thesis: rapid AI energy-efficiency gains per task, power and permitting constraints, social pushback, and a high-bandwidth memory shortage expected to persist through at least end-2027.

The US and EU no longer treat critical minerals as a purely commercial issue. Prices are often too low to build diversified supply, so governments use public finance, domestic mining and processing incentives, diversified-sourcing rules, bilateral deals, price floors and contracts for difference, and stockpiles.
Policy tool choice depends on market size: price floors are affordable in rare earths but too costly in copper, aluminium or steel, where trade measures (duties, import caps) are used instead.

The EU selected 93 strategic projects plus 13 in non-EU partner countries, with more than 2bn euros of public money mobilised. Korea Zinc plans a $7.4bn US smelter (trial operations in 2029), over 90% funded by the US government and strategic investors, including a $4.7bn DoW loan and a $0.21bn CHIPS Act grant.

The US launched Project Vault, a $12bn public-private stockpiling initiative, with Glencore and Mercuria committing $500mn each. The roughly $20bn of notional US copper inventories are privately funded and not part of Vault.

US copper stockpiling began when President Trump floated a refined copper tariff. Shipments overwhelmed the US market and pushed the CME curve into steep contango, which made warehouse financing profitable. A tariff ruling is expected before January 2027.

BofA's base case is that a no-tariff outcome would flatten the CME curve but would not cause a flood of copper to hit the market. Any time-spread volatility would be self-correcting, and the US government may prefer the status quo.
Producer countries are pushing the other way: UNCTAD counts nearly 100 new critical-mineral export measures since 2020 (DRC 18, China 16, Indonesia 12), aimed at forcing domestic processing.

The IEA estimates about $60bn of investment over a decade could diversify magnet rare-earth supply, against about $6.5tn of annual downstream sales exposed to disruption. Tripling rare-earth prices would add only about 0.1% to car costs.

Price forecasts: copper $13,000/t in 4Q26E rising to $16,000/t by 3Q27E, with 2026E at $13,331/t and 2027E at $15,500/t, and deficits expected in 2026 and 2027. Aluminium 2026E $3,600/t and 2027E $4,313/t.
Precious metals forecasts: gold $5,093/oz for 2026E and $4,925/oz for 2027E; silver $86/oz for 2026E and $74/oz for 2027E; platinum $2,476/oz for 2026E and $2,900/oz for 2027E.

Within the weekly moves, zinc rose 7.2% WoW on cash, copper 2.7%, aluminium 2.4%, and nickel fell 3.6%. Shanghai copper stocks fell 39.7% WoW to 44,612t, and LME copper cancelled warrants were 17.6% of stocks.

sector_views.rationale: Constrained ex-US availability, a deficit in 2026 and 2027, and electrification demand support prices, with upside seen into next year.
Consumers in Europe and the US are competing for units, supply additions have slowed because of China's 45Mt capacity cap, and deficits are expected in 2026 and 2027.
Gold is a hedge against US macro and policy uncertainty, and BofA sees upside risk to its forecasts.
The market has rebalanced on production discipline and new demand, though a technology shift in solar and possible substitution cloud the longer-run outlook.
Platinum remains in deficit and should outperform palladium.
Lead is tightly balanced, nickel swings from a 2026 deficit to a 2027 surplus, and zinc faces surpluses in 2026 and 2027.

earnings_insights: Freeport said on its recent results call that the sizable movement of product to US warehouses continues, resulting in tight market conditions in major consuming regions outside the US.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Weak Chinese consumption, driven by lower grid spending, but declines have started to bottom out.

macro_indicators.indicator: China FAI in electricity and heat generation
macro_indicators.interpretation: Slower grid investment reduces copper demand and makes China's 5-year plan electrification target harder to reach.
BofA says this could be the weakest since 1988.
A move to a deficit in 2027 underpins the bullish copper view.
Prices are supported by tight ex-US physical availability.

risk_factors: Copper downside: trade wars hurting sentiment, China re-exporting metal, and a sharp global demand slowdown into next year.
A US refined copper tariff decision that flattens the CME curve and releases warehoused metal, though BofA considers a flood unlikely.
AI and data centre efficiency gains, power and permitting constraints, social pushback and the high-bandwidth memory shortage could limit metals demand.
Gold downside: weaker investor sentiment, more positive real rates, a sustained USD rally, and scrap supply responding to high prices.
Silver risk: ETF liquidation, more supply, and faster substitution away from silver in solar.
Aluminium downside: no production discipline in China, higher Chinese exports, and trade war effects on sentiment.

vol_and_positioning: LME copper cash-to-3-month spreads have moved into deeper backwardation.
A single trader holds 50-79% of LME cash warrant positions, which makes the market easy to squeeze.
LME zinc inventories are very low, which has caused periodic short squeezes.
CME copper is in steep contango, which makes warehouse financing profitable. Consumers have been hedging while producers have been quieter, so liquidity is one-sided.
geopolitical: US and EU treat critical minerals access as a security issue, with heavy dependence on China for rare earths.
China's April 2025 restrictions on seven heavy rare earths and related magnets led some automakers to cut utilisation or stop production.
Export controls by producer countries: DRC (18 measures, including reduced cobalt exports), China (16), Indonesia (12, including limits on unprocessed ore exports).
A possible US refined copper tariff, with a ruling expected before January 2027.
The report cites an Iran war slowing demand in Europe and the US, and Middle East supply disruptions affecting aluminium.
Brazil signed Law No. 15,506/2026 on 16 September 2026, creating a National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals.
The US signed 11 bilateral frameworks at its February 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial.

tension_points.bull_case: US stockpiling and profitable warehouse financing keep metal out of ex-US markets, and LME backwardation and concentrated positioning could trigger squeezes. BofA sees copper upside into next year.
tension_points.bear_case: If the US decides against a refined copper tariff, the CME curve would flatten, financing deals would lose profitability and warehoused copper could come out, pressuring nearby prices.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A US decision not to impose a refined copper tariff (ruling expected before January 2027) that flattens the CME curve and releases metal. BofA considers a flood unlikely.

theme_stances.key_argument: Profitable US warehouse financing has drawn spare copper to the US, leaving the rest of the world short despite weak Chinese demand.
theme_stances.evidence: constrained availability should continue to support copper prices

theme_stances.key_argument: Hyperscale data centres are considerably more metals intensive than enterprise sites, adding to copper, aluminium and silver demand.
theme_stances.evidence: hyperscalers are considerably more metals intensive than traditional enterprise data centres

theme_stances.key_argument: Governments are prepared to pay a mineral-security premium because diversification costs are small relative to the economic activity at risk.
theme_stances.evidence: governments are increasingly prepared to pay a mineral-security premium
